sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the purpose, typical contents, and use of encounter forms (superbills) in a medical office.
- Explain charge capture and how captured charges flow into claims generation.
- Describe the claims generation and submission process, including claim forms, electronic transactions, and clean-claim requirements.
- Explain how codes are accurately assigned from documentation, including the assistant's role in supporting documentation integrity and escalating discrepancies.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the encounter form like a restaurant server's order ticket: it lists everything the patient received that day so the office knows what to bill for.

### Question 2

Checking boxes on the encounter form is like ticking items on a shopping list — it writes down what happened so a bill can be made.

### Question 3

The encounter form is like a pre-filled menu of the most common services, so the provider just checks the ones that apply.

### Question 4

The encounter form is like the recipe card the cook hands to the billing clerk — if the recipe is wrong, the dish (claim) comes out wrong.

### Question 5

If the order ticket seems to be missing items, you don't guess and write them in yourself — you ask the person who knows what was served.

### Question 6

A claim needs the 'who' (the patient) and the 'what' (the services and diagnoses) to build a correct bill.

### Question 7

Electronic records turn the paper ticket into a screen where the visit's services and diagnoses are captured digitally.

### Question 8

Charge capture is like writing down every item a customer bought so nothing gets left off the bill.

### Question 9

If the server forgets to write down your drink, the restaurant can't charge you for it and loses that money.

### Question 10

A charge is a pair: the diagnosis code says 'why' and the procedure code says 'what was done.'

### Question 11

The diagnosis is the reason 'why' the service happened — like showing a receipt for why you bought something.

### Question 12

The encounter form is a quick notes sheet for billing, but the full story lives in the patient's chart.

### Question 13

Checking the schedule against the tickets is like making sure every table that sat down turned in an order.

### Question 14

If the notes say more happened than the ticket shows, you ask the person who knows instead of guessing or changing numbers yourself.

### Question 15

If the ticket never makes it to the kitchen, the order never gets cooked or billed.

### Question 16

Charge capture lag is how long the bill 'sits on the counter' before it gets entered.

### Question 17

If you wait too long to turn in the order ticket, the kitchen's cutoff passes and the order can't go out.

### Question 18

The assistant is like the runner who makes sure every ticket is filled in and delivered — not the chef who decides what goes on the plate.

### Question 19

Comparing the ticket to the chart is like checking the receipt against what's in the bag — they should match.

### Question 20

If the receipt lists something that isn't in the bag, you fix the receipt — you don't pretend the item is there.

### Question 21

ICD-10-CM is the 'why' code — it names the problem the patient has.

### Question 22

CPT is the 'what was done' code — the procedure or service the patient received.

### Question 23

The CMS-1500 is the standard 'bill' doctors' offices use to ask insurance to pay for an outpatient visit.

### Question 24

Hospitals and facilities use a different 'bill form' (UB-04) than a doctor's office (CMS-1500).

### Question 25

The 837P is the electronic version of the doctor's bill, sent by computer instead of paper.

### Question 26

The 837I is the hospital's electronic bill, matching the UB-04 paper form.

### Question 27

The NPI is like a provider's official ID badge number that must appear on every bill.

### Question 28

The clearinghouse is like a mailroom that checks each envelope and routes it to the right address.

### Question 29

A clean claim is like a homework paper with no mistakes — it can be graded right away without being sent back.

### Question 30

A claim missing a required code is like a letter with no address — it can't be delivered and processed.

### Question 31

Scrubbing is like proofreading a letter before mailing it so the post office doesn't send it back.

### Question 32

Adjudication is the insurance company 'grading' the bill and deciding how much to pay.

### Question 33

After the bill is graded, the insurance company sends back a report card showing what it paid and why.

### Question 34

A claim needs real billing facts — who, when, what — not personal trivia like a favorite color.

### Question 35

The diagnosis is the 'reason' line on the bill — without it, the insurance can't decide if it should pay.

### Question 36

The insurance company has a 'due date' for receiving the bill; miss it and they won't pay.

### Question 37

Different insurance companies have different 'due dates,' just like different teachers have different deadlines.

### Question 38

Charge capture is gathering the ingredients; claims generation is baking the cake from them.

### Question 39

It's easier to fix a typo before you mail the letter than after it comes back refused.

### Question 40

Checking your homework before turning it in is how you get it right the first time.

### Question 41

The provider's signature is like signing a school permission slip — it says 'I stand behind this.'

### Question 42

The place-of-service code is the 'where' — living room vs. doctor's office changes how it's billed.

### Question 43

The acknowledgment is like a delivery-tracking number — it tells you the package arrived and where it is.

### Question 44

The insurance is saying, 'The reason you gave doesn't match the service you billed.'

### Question 45

When you're not sure, you ask the teacher instead of writing down a guess on the test.

### Question 46

The ABN is a 'heads up' note telling a Medicare patient, 'This might not be paid, and here's your choice.'

### Question 47

Using an old map gets you lost; using old codes gets your claim rejected.

### Question 48

The assistant can type in and send the carefully prepared bill, but doesn't change the recipe to make it pay more.

### Question 49

A wrong ID number is like putting the wrong address on a package — it won't get to the right place.

### Question 50

Code from the paper trail, not from guessing — like answering test questions only from the book.

### Question 51

If the receipt shows an item that isn't in the bag, you don't charge for it until you confirm it's really there.

### Question 52

A query is politely asking the doctor, 'Can you clarify what you did so we code it correctly?'

### Question 53

If the book doesn't contain the answer you're citing, that's a clue your citation is wrong.

### Question 54

Saying 'broken arm' is less helpful than 'broken left forearm near the wrist' — details matter.

### Question 55

Upcoding is like claiming you ran 10 miles when you only ran 3.

### Question 56

If someone asks you to change the answer to get a better grade, the right move is to say no and tell a trusted adult.

### Question 57

The diagnosis code comes from the doctor's written findings, not from guessing or copying.

### Question 58

You can't fill in the test answer before the doctor has actually examined the patient — that's guessing.

### Question 59

Documentation is the 'show your work' that proves the service was actually needed.

### Question 60

The payer checks that the 'why' and the 'what' match up like a puzzle.

### Question 61

The assistant helps the teacher keep the answer key (chart) complete and clear, but doesn't grade the test.

### Question 62

If you can't read the teacher's writing, you ask the teacher — you don't guess the answer.

### Question 63

You record what actually happened, not what would pay best — honesty over profit.

### Question 64

Billing for something that isn't in the record is like charging for work you didn't do — it gets you in trouble.

### Question 65

If you accidentally undercounted, you fix the count to match the truth — you don't invent extra items.

### Question 66

Changing the record is like erasing and rewriting history — it makes the whole story unreliable.

### Question 67

Fix the answer to match the book, not the book to match the answer.

### Question 68

The best way to pass an inspection is to keep things correct all along, not to tidy up at the last minute.

### Question 69

It's a relay race: run the visit, write the ticket, make the bill, send it, get graded, then record the payment.

### Question 70

Each department is a different store in the same mall — each one must ring up its own sale for the same customer.

### Question 71

Checking the attendance sheet against the tickets shows if any customer was served but never billed.

### Question 72

The scrubber checks that the 'ID badge number' on the bill is real before mailing it.

### Question 73

If the address is wrong, look it up and fix it — don't just re-mail the same envelope.

### Question 74

If every student's homework is word-for-word identical, a teacher suspects copying.

### Question 75

Check the receipt first, and if you can't explain it, ask the billing team before telling the customer anything for certain.

### Question 76

Charging only for what really happened keeps the books honest — like a store that rings up exactly what you bought.

### Question 77

The full story in the chart is the real evidence; the form is just a quick summary.

### Question 78

Copying the same answer for every question looks fast but isn't true for each patient.

### Question 79

A modifier is a small note on the bill that says 'by the way, this was a special case' when it truly was.

### Question 80

Coding turns the doctor's story into a short set of standard numbers so computers and insurers can process it.

### Question 81

The code must be a perfect fit for what the chart says, like the right puzzle piece.

### Question 82

The 'when' is as important as the 'what' — the bill must say when each thing happened.

### Question 83

When something doesn't look right, you stop and ask the person in charge instead of guessing.
